On the facade of the main building of the US Post Office in New York (the Farley Building), a sentence is engraved that you may have seen before in photos: "Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds." The sentence was engraved in 1914 and is so famous that many consider it the official motto of the US Postal Service. In his book "Neither Snow Nor Rain," which is dedicated to the history of the US Postal Service, David Leonard tells the story behind this sentence. The sentence was used by Herodotus in his famous book, Histories, to describe the Iranian couriers during the era of Darius the Great. The Iranian postal industry began during the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great and reached its peak during the era of Darius the Great, and was known as the fastest organized postal system in the world (the Egyptians and Chinese also had postal systems, but the symbol of fast and organized mail was Iran). Leonard ends the story of how this sentence was chosen and engraved as follows: Many think this sentence is the motto of the US Postal Service. But this sentence is merely the homage of the world's greatest postal system to one of its most renowned ancestors. #هایلایت

One.
The owner of himself always grieves and melts.

(Saadi)
When we consider ourselves our own owner, we melt from grief. When we consider the kingdom and the owned to belong to that beautiful Unique One, we become free and liberated. "Inna lillah" means we belong to Him. We are not our own owners.

▫️Two.
Every foot that entered the house found a treasure;
No longer would all its life be at the market.
(Saadi)
There is a treasure that is found in the realm of the heart. One who finds the way to the inner treasure is freed from dependence on markets. Bayazid Bastami said about the meaning of dervishhood: "The one who, in the corner of his own heart, finds a foot entering a treasure..."

▫️Three.
One who became a stranger to wealth and greatness and lordship,
Is familiar to whomever he reaches.
(Saadi)
One who sees himself free from names and positions and passing powers can be familiar and close to everyone. If we are captivated by our own greatness and lordship and wealth, if we are bound by our position and name and reputation and intelligence and knowledge, we lose the felicity of "familiarity."

▫️Four.
Whoever does not know gratitude for today's blessing
Will eat regret upon the portion of tomorrow's mercy.
(Saadi)
One who does not appreciate the gifts of this world and does not welcome them with gratitude and joy will also be deprived of the mercy of the next world.

Whoever does not see today in the world the countenance of the Friend,
It is most likely that tomorrow he will have no vision.
(Saadi)
The beauty of nature and the movement and growth of the earth is a mercy of this world:
"Fa-unzur ila athar rahmatillah kayfa yuhyi al-arda ba'da mawtiha" (Surah Rum, verse 50)
"Look at these signs of Allah's kindness, how He revives the earth after its death." (Translation of Tafsir Kashf al-Asrar)

▫️Five.
Except the remembrance of the Friend, whatever you do is wasted life;
Except the secret of love, whatever you say is vanity.
(Saadi)
If life is not mixed with the remembrance of the Friend, and is not spent in longing for the Friend, it is wasted. It has passed in vanity:
Saadi, if he does not risk love, what shall he do with the kingdom of existence?
It is a pity that a whole life should go to waste.

The remembrance and recollection of the Friend has no end. It is not tiresome either. Because it is the food of the soul. The bread and water of the soul:
Our speech grew long and still remains,
For the remembrance of the Friend brings no weariness whatsoever.
(Saadi)
Therefore, his regret is for the times that passed unaware of the Friend:
Whatever we said other than the tale of the Friend,
In all our life we regret it.
(Saadi)
If there is any regret, it is nothing but this: why did we not breathe in His remembrance more? Why did we not throb in longing for Him more?
So that precious life does not end in regret,
All night Your remembrance was ongoing and repeated.

Speaking with Him, speaking of Him, and floating in the "tale of the Friend" is the meaning of life.

🔸The Loss of a Mediator🔸

If we were to describe any figure with a single word, the word that fits Ayatollah Seyyed Mousa Shubeyri Zanjani (who passed away last night) is "mediator."

Despite being considered, in terms of his jurisprudential orientation, among the traditionalist jurists of the seminary, and despite not being devoid of taste or conviction in politics and history—as is evident from his scattered remarks and writings (including in the highly readable book collection "A Sip from the Sea")—he had his own distinct and particular social and political demeanor. In the past two or three decades, he played a role that others were incapable of fulfilling: the role of "mediator" between the system and the religious currents and individuals it had cast out. Shubeyri Zanjani was a "dragoman" for translating the words of two groups who did not understand each other's language. That is why knots that could not be untied through law and conventional political methods were sometimes loosened by a single phone call from him, and challenges that could have spiraled into crises were sometimes defused by a single piece of advice from him. These mediations were, of course, typically behind the scenes and never publicized—and that, too, was part of his way of being.

Because of this role he played, Shubeyri was beloved by all sides. He both associated with the martyred Leader and would recite the funeral prayer for clerics critical of the system, and the door of his home remained open every day to all political and religious currents. Undoubtedly, his humble and tolerant character also contributed to this.

In religious matters as well, although he is classified among the traditional jurists, he took a different approach there too. Unlike them, he did not use his position, standing, and influence to pursue religious identity-driven concerns, and did not seek to pile up a calendar of Shia occasions and to fatten rituals. On the contrary, he was critical of the excessive expansion of rituals.

That said, if the loss of Mr. Shubeyri Zanjani is considered a scholarly loss for the seminaries, it will be a functional and institutional blow for the system and for Iranian society as well—one that could disrupt the relations between the system and certain seminary and religious currents. Although Shubeyri was not considered among the first-tier maraji' in terms of the organizational structure of the marja'iyya, and did not have extensive organizations and numerous offices, and the number of his followers did not extend beyond the circle of certain seminary elites and his fellow townspeople, his loss creates a void in the institution of Shia marja'iyya in Iran that cannot be filled—especially in the current critical conditions, when Iranian society, more than ever, needs those who play the role of mediator in various arenas.

The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today through the mirror of history. In writing this play, rather than seeking to construct a mythical figure of Cyrus, I have thought about a human being who, amid power, violence, and fear, faces a difficult choice: the sword or the word. History, for me, is not a mass of names and conquests; it is the memory of the people who lived in it; people who were afraid, who loved, who betrayed, who stood firm, and who made choices at fateful moments. "Cyrus" is an attempt to hear the silenced voices of these very people; to see the human beings who have sometimes been forgotten behind the great names of history. As a director, too, I have not wanted to reconstruct history; I have wanted to summon it into the present; so that perhaps we may realize that the distance between that era and our era is not as far as we think. "Cyrus" is not the narrative of a conqueror; it is the search for a human being who wants to take power beyond the mere meaning of domination. Perhaps that is why, for me, "Cyrus" is more about the possibility of remaining human in the midst of power than about the past.#نادر_برهانی_مرند@moaser_theater
